title: Utz et al. (2002) True/False Quiz
instructions: Choose True or False by checking each statement's scope, direction, and timing. Distinguish formal and informal participation, observed associations and proposed explanations, and the main six-month analysis and later follow-up findings.

items.prompt: The study defined social participation as social interaction with people other than one's spouse.
items.explanation: The construct included formal roles, such as volunteering and religious or group participation, and informal interaction, such as contact with friends or relatives outside the marital relationship.

items.prompt: Activity theory identifies preservation of preloss participation levels as the central adaptation after losing spouse-related roles.
items.explanation: Activity theory emphasizes replacing lost roles with new, compensatory activities to preserve identity. Maintaining earlier patterns and levels of participation is closer to the continuity hypothesis described in the article.

items.prompt: The frequent use of female-only samples in earlier bereavement research limited the ability to assess gender differences in adjustment.
items.explanation: The authors identify female-only samples as one of four methodological reasons for inconsistent findings. Such samples cannot directly compare adjustment patterns in widows and widowers.

items.prompt: For respondents who became widowed, the timing of Wave 1 was set relative to their baseline interview date.
items.explanation: Wave 1 occurred six months after the spouse's death, not six months after baseline. The researchers controlled for the varying number of months between baseline and Wave 1; matched controls were interviewed at comparable times.

items.prompt: Depression was measured at baseline, like the other confounding variables described in the methods.
items.explanation: Depression was measured at Wave 1. The other listed confounding variables were baseline measures, so depression should not be treated as a preloss control measured at the same time as those variables.

items.prompt: CLOC eligibility was restricted to noninstitutionalized, English-speaking married couples in which the husband was at least 65 years old.
items.explanation: These are the eligibility conditions given in the methods. The age requirement applied to the husband; it should not be expanded into a claim that every respondent, including every wife, was at least 65.

items.prompt: The informal participation index had a reported reliability of α = .52, while the formal participation index had α = .71.
items.explanation: The two-item informal index covered getting together and telephone contact. The three-item formal index covered volunteering, group meetings, and religious services. Their reported alpha values were .52 and .71, respectively.

items.prompt: In the baseline regressions, people who later became widowed had higher informal participation than those who remained married.
items.explanation: Those who later became widowed had lower baseline informal participation, with a reported coefficient of −.29 (p ≤ .01). The difference preceded the death and should not be described as an effect of a death that had already occurred.

items.prompt: The widowhood-by-sex interaction was significant, indicating different average associations of widowhood with participation for women and men.
items.explanation: The interaction was not significant in any model. The authors interpreted this as suggesting similar average patterns for widows and widowers, rather than evidence of a gender difference or proof that the associations were exactly equal.

items.prompt: Poor or fair spousal health at baseline was associated with lower baseline informal participation.
items.explanation: The baseline informal-participation regression reported a negative coefficient for poor or fair spousal health (−.31, p ≤ .001). This is a preloss association, not a randomized estimate of the effect of spousal illness.

items.prompt: In the analysis accompanying Figure 2, widows reported a greater increase than widowers in friends' and relatives' interest in contacting them.
items.explanation: The authors found no apparent sex difference in these reports. The contact-interest responses suggested that friends and relatives may have initiated additional support; they did not establish who caused the observed participation patterns.
items.source: Gender patterns in reported contact interest

items.prompt: The authors reported similar coefficients in additional 18-month models, suggesting that the informal-participation pattern observed at six months persisted beyond the initial follow-up.
items.explanation: The main table reports six-month outcomes. The authors describe similar findings from identical models at 18 months, with those results not shown in a table. This supports their interpretation of persistence, not a claim that the main analysis covered all later follow-ups.

items.prompt: Among widowed respondents, 71% reported the same interest in contact with relatives and friends as when their spouse was alive.
items.explanation: Reported interest was higher for 17%, unchanged for 71%, and lower for 12%. These figures describe preferences for contact, not percentages whose actual activity levels changed by the same amount.

items.prompt: The authors concluded that combining the three classical theories adequately explains the diversity and unfolding process of adjustment to widowhood.
items.explanation: Although continuity received the strongest support among the three, none was wholly supported or wholly refuted. The authors considered developmental and middle-range perspectives more promising for capturing diverse trajectories and changes over the life course.

items.prompt: Support efforts could reach people with ailing spouses and couples facing an impending death, as well as those recently bereaved.
items.explanation: Because social withdrawal may begin before the loss, the authors proposed outreach during a spouse's final stage of life as well as after death. This is a practical implication of the findings, not a tested intervention result.
